worst_places.quote: JavaScript is render-blocking by default and should be deferred to the end of the body or use async/defer attributes. CSS must load before render, images are loaded asynchronously, and fonts can use font-display to avoid blocking.
worst_places.problem: quiz-19 (id web-performance-quiz-14). The question asks which resource is 'most commonly render-blocking'; the key is JavaScript. The explanation's own second sentence ('CSS must load before render') says the opposite of its own key, and both contradict the articles: en/02-performance-metrics.md says 'The browser paints nothing until all CSS ... have loaded', and en/08 states 'CSS blocks rendering (CSSOM must be built before Render Tree); JS blocks DOM construction'. It also teaches the obsolete 'move scripts before </body>' advice that bank q-16 and article 03 replace with defer/async. A reader who learns this item will answer the interview question wrongly.
worst_places.before: JavaScript is render-blocking by default and should be deferred to the end of the body or use async/defer attributes. CSS must load before render, images are loaded asynchronously, and fonts can use font-display to avoid blocking.
worst_places.after: A synchronous <script> in <head> is parser-blocking: the browser stops building the DOM until the script has downloaded and run, so the first paint is delayed too. CSS is the truly render-blocking resource — the browser paints nothing until the CSSOM is built. The modern fix for scripts is defer (run after HTML is parsed, in document order) or async (run as soon as it arrives, order not guaranteed); moving the tag before </body> is the old workaround for the same problem. Images load asynchronously and never block the first paint; fonts use font-display to avoid blocking text.

worst_places.quote: `preconnect` opens the DNS lookup, TCP handshake, and TLS negotiation for a third-party origin ahead of time, so the actual request that follows is faster - use it for domains you know you'll hit soon (a font CDN, an analytics endpoint) but sparingly, since each preconnect opens a real connection and holds it; more than 4-6 wastes bandwidth.
worst_places.problem: q-2, the answer's opening sentence: 137 words in one sentence (the whole first paragraph is one period), carrying four unrelated facts and three unexpanded acronyms (DNS, TCP, TLS, CDN) before the reader has been told what a resource hint is. On a phone this is a 12-line block with no place to pause. 100 of the 165 sentences in the EN bank (60.6%) are over the 25-word threshold; this is the worst of them.
worst_places.before: `preconnect` opens the DNS lookup, TCP handshake, and TLS negotiation for a third-party origin ahead of time, so the actual request that follows is faster - use it for domains you know you'll hit soon (a font CDN, an analytics endpoint) but sparingly, since each preconnect opens a real connection and holds it; more than 4-6 wastes bandwidth.
worst_places.after: `preconnect` warms up a connection to another domain before you actually need it. It does the three slow steps up front: DNS lookup (turning the domain name into an IP address), the TCP handshake, and the TLS handshake for HTTPS. When the real request finally goes out, the connection is already open, so it is much faster. Use it for domains you know you will hit soon — a font CDN, an analytics endpoint. Use it sparingly: each `preconnect` opens a real connection and holds it open, so more than 4-6 of them just wastes bandwidth.

worst_places.quote: The browser must complete Parse → Compile → Render → Paint → Composite within 16ms. Use `requestAnimationFrame` for animations, batch DOM changes, avoid layout thrashing by reading then writing DOM properties, and leverage GPU acceleration with `transform` and `opacity`.
worst_places.problem: q-21, and the same shape in q-22 to q-25 (all five 'advanced' entries). These are a completely different tier from q-1 to q-20: a 2-sentence checklist of imperatives with nothing explained, versus 400-word answers with worked examples. Five techniques are named in one sentence with no example between them, and terms are dumped raw (q-24: HOL, HPACK, QUIC, 0-RTT, UDP, RTT; q-25: RUM, p50/p75/p95). The pipeline it names also does not match article 06, which teaches Style → Layout → Paint → Composite.
worst_places.before: The browser must complete Parse → Compile → Render → Paint → Composite within 16ms. Use `requestAnimationFrame` for animations, batch DOM changes, avoid layout thrashing by reading then writing DOM properties, and leverage GPU acceleration with `transform` and `opacity`.
worst_places.after:
At 60 frames per second the browser has 16ms to produce each frame, and it has to fit the whole pipeline into that window: Style (which CSS rules apply) → Layout (sizes and positions) → Paint (fill in pixels) → Composite (glue the layers together). Miss the budget and the frame is dropped, which the user sees as stutter.

Four things keep you inside it. Schedule visual work with `requestAnimationFrame`, so it runs once at the start of a frame instead of at a random moment. Batch DOM writes together instead of interleaving them with reads. Avoid layout thrashing: read all the layout properties you need first, then do all the writes — alternating read/write forces the browser to recompute layout on every single read. And animate only `transform` and `opacity`, because those two skip Layout and Paint entirely and run on the GPU.

worst_places.quote: - **"fetchpriority="high" is the same as preload"** — they're different things. `preload` says "download this resource now, regardless of whether you'll encounter it in the document." `fetchpriority` says "when you download this already-known resource, do it at this priority." `preload` changes when discovery happens; `fetchpriority` changes the priority of a resource the browser already knows about.
worst_places.problem: Line 439. 55 words in one bullet, built as quote-inside-quote-inside-bullet with three nested levels of punctuation, and it ends by restating the same contrast a second time. The RU version of the same bullet is 46 words with the same structure. Every article ends with a «Типичные ошибки на интервью» list built this way, and these bullets are consistently the longest sentences in each file — the one place where the otherwise short-sentence style of the articles breaks down.
worst_places.before: `preload` says "download this resource now, regardless of whether you'll encounter it in the document." `fetchpriority` says "when you download this already-known resource, do it at this priority." `preload` changes when discovery happens; `fetchpriority` changes the priority of a resource the browser already knows about.
worst_places.after: They answer different questions. `preload` answers *when*: start downloading this file now, even if the browser has not met it in the document yet. `fetchpriority` answers *how urgently*: the browser already knows about this file, so put it higher or lower in the queue.

The question bank writes one mega-sentence per idea instead of one sentence per fact. Every answer in q-1..q-20 is exactly three prose paragraphs, and each paragraph is one or two sentences of 70-160 words that chain a definition, two or three sub-cases, a caveat and a recommendation with dashes and semicolons (q-12: 158 words, q-2: 137, q-13: 116, q-19: 95). 60.6% of EN sentences and 53.3% of RU sentences are over the length threshold.
